children.text: A self-hosted platform instead of the glue between your CMS, your data and your systems.

children.html: Configure it instead of coding it. No code for the people who use it. Security and governance controls built in, with the tests and their results in the open. MIT licence, one organisation per installation, no per-user fee.

children.html: MIT · self-hosted · version 0.2.0 · no per-user fee

Most organisations that publish and integrate end up with four things stitched together: a content platform, a page builder, a library for files, and a layer of scripts and connectors to the systems they already own. Each has its own users, its own secrets, its own upgrades.
Whoobe is one installation with one data model, one gateway to your systems, one media library and one editor, run by the team that owns it.

children.html: Point the gateway at an OpenAPI file or a sample request: routes, response shapes and fields appear in the editor, and a block can show the data. The credentials stay on the server.

children.css: flex-1 gap-3 rounded-xl glass-panel bg-[#1A1D24]/70 border border-white/10 p-6

children.text: No code for the people who use it

children.html: Editors build pages from blocks, snippets and kits. A data manager adds a field to a class without a deploy. Nobody on the content side asks a developer to move a button or to publish.

children.css: flex-1 gap-3 rounded-xl glass-panel bg-[#1A1D24]/70 border border-white/10 p-6

children.text: Security controls, and the proof behind them

children.html: An append-only audit log, mandatory two-factor authentication by role, single sign-on with OpenID Connect, encrypted credentials, data subject tools and retention, metrics. We do not certify our own code: we say what we tested, publish the results, failures included, and list what is not covered.

children.text: Open source means showing the work

children.html: The code is MIT and public. So are the tests, the findings (open and closed), the results of every release, failures included, and the plans that say how it is built, including the use of an AI assistant. We do not ask you to trust a claim: we put what backs it where you can open it.

Version 0.2.0, a 0. series: behaviour can change between minor releases, and the release notes say what. One OpenID Connect provider, no SAML or LDAP, no high availability yet. The limits are on one page, not in the small print.

children.text: What the tests do not tell you

children.html: A green run means that these checks passed on this code, at this commit. It does not mean that there are no vulnerabilities. It is not an audit, a penetration test or a certification, and there has not been an outside one: all the work is ours.

The coverage has holes, and they are listed: SQL fuzzing of most endpoints, the impact of prompt injection on the AI features, a full Content-Security-Policy for the admin and the editor, a live host with a public certificate, and load testing (by design).

children.text: Where the results are, and they stay public

children.html: Open source earns the name by showing its work. The tests, the findings, the results of every release and the plans are in the repository or in its public history. The failures are published too: on the day of release 0.2.0, two runs failed before the green one, and both are in the record.

docs/plans
If a claim on this site is not backed by something you can open, ask in GitHub Discussions. A vulnerability goes the other way, privately: see the security policy, never a public discussion.

One OpenID Connect provider at a time. It was tried against Keycloak; Microsoft Entra, Okta and Google follow the same standard and have not been tried. SAML and LDAP are not built: a broker in front covers them.
The audit log records successful actions. A refused attempt is not in it.
Two-factor authentication, the password policy and retention are off until you set them. An upgrade changes nothing by itself.
No high availability. One installation, one database; recovery is by backup and restore.
No third-party certification (ISO 27001, SOC 2) and no outside penetration test.
It is a 0. series: behaviour can change between minor releases. The release notes list what.

pages.title: Run it
pages.description: What runs, how it is organised, upgrades, backups, observability and who Whoobe is for. Containers, PostgreSQL and an S3-compatible store.

sections.css: w-full px-6 pt-20 pb-14 bg-[#12151B] border-b border-white/10

children.html: Run it
children.css: text-base leading-relaxed [&_a]:text-[#A78BFA] [&_a]:underline [&_a]:underline-offset-2 [&_a:hover]:text-white [&_strong]:text-white text-xs font-semibold tracking-widest uppercase text-cyan-400

children.text: Built to be run by a small team.

children.html: Whoobe is containers, a PostgreSQL database and an S3-compatible object store. No licence server, no per-user fee, no call home.

Five application services (API, asset service, gateway, dashboard, editor), PostgreSQL 16 and an object store (Garage in the default stack; any S3-compatible store, or a managed one, in production). Docker Compose is the way it is deployed and documented. Architecture →

One organisation per installation. A company with several sites uses one installation and several websites; an agency uses one workspace per client. Roles follow functions (editor, publisher, administrator), not people. Creating workspaces →
Upgrades: migrations are additions only, applied when the API starts; the release notes list behaviour changes; take a backup first. Upgrade and migrations →
Backups and recovery: encrypted database backups, restore scripts and a rehearsal; the nightly job pulled by another machine, with a freshness check, comes with the next release. Scheduling backups →
Observability: health, metrics, logs. Observability →
What it takes: the skills and the hours, estimated, by task and by frequency. Skills and effort →
No call home: no telemetry, no analytics, no licence check; nothing is sent to the authors.
